name: Unlawful possession of firearm (finite-term marriage-dissolution protective order)
conduct: Possessing a firearm after receiving notice of a qualifying order and before that order expires. The prosecution must establish the actual order, its statutory authority, its continuing effect and receipt of notice; being described as a respondent or defendant alone establishes none of these. The applicable culpable mental state and voluntary possession rules also apply: actual care, custody, control or management is not established by mere proximity. The statutory firearm definition and antique/replica exclusion apply. Section 46.04(c) excludes a legally defined peace officer actively employed as a sworn, full-time paid employee of a state agency or political subdivision; a license, former office or reserve title alone does not establish every condition. The predicate is a protective order rendered under Family Code §6.504 in a marriage-dissolution suit, using Subtitle B, Title 4; a routine divorce injunction or a pending divorce alone is not the specified predicate. Section 85.004 requires a separate protective-order document. The order’s current expiration controls. Section 85.025(a) provides the stated period of up to two years, or two years after issuance when no period is stated, only subject to the section’s other duration rules. Under (a-2), when the respondent is a party to a marriage-dissolution suit and the applicant or a member of the applicant’s family or household is the other party, the order continues until two years after the judge approves and signs the final divorce decree. Under (a-3), when those persons are parties to a suit affecting the parent-child relationship, it continues until two years after the court renders the final order in that suit. Under (a-4), when the respondent is charged with a family-violence offense under Penal Code Title 5 or an offense under §25.11, it continues until two years after final disposition of the criminal case. These periods run from the specified later event, not from issuance; the order may therefore remain effective more than two years after issuance. Subsection (a-1) permits specified longer periods, and (c) provides confinement-related extensions. The applicable version must be checked for the order’s rendition date: S.B. 1120’s 2025 Chapter 85 changes apply only to orders rendered on or after September 1, 2025; earlier orders remain governed by their then-applicable law. A motion seeking review does not itself terminate the order. Agreed and default orders have their own statutory conditions; agreement or nonappearance is not an automatic exemption. No protected person can authorize ignoring an operative order. This choice covers only a finite-term order in the specified category; lifetime, indefinite and ex-parte-only orders are outside this choice’s reviewed scope, not declared lawful to disregard. Finite duration is a selection boundary, not an added statutory element or proof of constitutional validity. The actual process, findings, duration, later modifications and constitutional application require examination. Rahimi upheld the federal restriction in its temporary credible-threat setting; it did not approve every Texas order. Noyes vacated and remanded a lifetime-order judgment for further proceedings after Rahimi, rather than categorically invalidating §46.04(c). Do not infer that an order has ended or may be ignored from this summary. Separate federal firearm restrictions are not determined here.
penalty: Class A misdemeanor under §46.04(e): ordinarily up to one year in jail, a fine up to $4,000, or both. Section 46.11 can increase punishment to the next offense category if its knowledge and school-zone/function findings are proved beyond a reasonable doubt; no such findings are assumed here. Qualifying priors and case-specific findings can change punishment.
